name: Maxillomandibular advancement (MMA)

card.summary: Surgery that moves both jaws forward, established as a sleep-apnoea operation and marketed online as a looks-plus-airway upgrade.
card.aka: MMA, bimaxillary advancement, Bi-Max, maxillomandibular osteotomy (MMO)
card.note: The strong evidence is for sleep apnoea, not appearance; lower-facial numbness is very common early on and hardware removal is reported in a fifth of patients.

quick.overview:
Maxillomandibular advancement (MMA) is jaw surgery in which the upper and lower jaws are both cut and moved forward, enlarging the space behind the tongue and soft palate. It was developed within orthognathic surgery and is now one of the most studied surgical treatments for obstructive sleep apnoea, usually considered after other treatments such as CPAP or other sleep surgery have not worked.

In looksmaxxing communities, MMA and bimax are discussed as a way to advance the face and sometimes to fix breathing at the same time, with threads about rotation, midface expansion and surgeon choice. Sleep-apnoea outcomes are well documented in meta-analyses; evidence on cosmetic outcomes is much thinner.
quick.mechanism: A Le Fort I osteotomy frees the upper jaw and a mandibular osteotomy, typically a sagittal split, frees the lower jaw; both are advanced and fixed with plates and screws. Advancing the skeleton also pulls forward the soft tissues attached to it, widening the airway at the palate and tongue base.
quick.risks: A 2025 meta-analysis found early lower-facial numbness in about 83 percent of patients, persisting beyond a year in about a third, and hardware removal in about 22 percent. Other documented concerns include bleeding, airway swelling after surgery, relapse, jaw-joint problems and a longer recovery than other sleep surgeries.

lead: Maxillomandibular advancement (MMA), also called bimaxillary advancement, bimax or Bi-Max, is a jaw operation that moves both the upper jaw (maxilla) and the lower jaw (mandible) forward and fixes them in the new position [1]. Because the skin, lips, cheeks and chin are attached to the skeleton, advancing the jaws also moves the soft tissues, which is why people interested in facial appearance discuss it as a way to build forward projection of the lower face while enlarging the airway behind the tongue and palate [3][14]. It originated in orthognathic surgery for facial skeletal deformity and bite problems and was later applied to obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA), where it is classed as a type of sleep surgery [1][22].

For sleep apnoea, MMA is described in reviews as one of the most effective surgical options and a surgical choice for refractory disease [1][5]. A 2025 meta-analysis of 31 studies and 1,597 patients reported a mean fall in apnoea-hypopnoea index of about 42 events per hour, alongside high rates of lower-facial numbness and of hardware removal [3]. A 2026 narrative review describes an approximately 80 percent reduction in the index and frames MMA as a treatment for selected patients, including those who cannot tolerate or adhere to CPAP [27]. A 2023 meta-analysis of appearance outcomes pooled a satisfaction rate of 94.2 percent with facial aesthetics after MMA, in patient, surgeon and layperson raters [24].

In looksmaxxing communities, MMA and bimax are mentioned as surgeries that may combine facial advancement with an airway benefit, and users discuss how they interact with other procedures such as maxillary skeletal expansion and who the well-known surgeons are [14]. Published research on MMA is dominated by sleep-apnoea outcomes; cosmetic-only use is addressed mainly through the broader orthognathic literature and the satisfaction studies above [22][24].

paras: MMA enlarges the upper airway by physically moving the facial skeleton forward, taking the soft palate, tongue and surrounding muscles with it.[3] It is often performed with genioglossus advancement, which pulls the tongue base forward.[1] In the Stanford protocol of sleep surgery, MMA is described as the second phase of treatment.[2]
Technology such as virtual surgical planning and 3D printing has made planning more efficient, and a surgery-first approach has grown in popularity for malocclusion cases.[5]

Review articles describe the operation as combining a maxillary (Le Fort I) osteotomy with a mandibular osteotomy and fixation, with treatment planning that includes the degree of movement and timing of surgery; patient evaluation includes history, clinical and radiographic examination, endoscopy and polysomnography [1]. Orthodontic preparation followed by surgery has been the traditional sequence for complex cases, while a surgery-first approach has grown because of shorter treatment time and improved quality of life [5]. Counter-clockwise rotation of the occlusal plane is a planning technique studied for how it affects the amount of mandibular advancement and pharynx shape [12]. A 2020 review covers skeletal surgery options for sleep apnoea more broadly [16].

Planning decisions described in the literature include how far each jaw is moved, whether the occlusal plane is rotated, whether the chin (genioplasty) or tongue base is treated, and how the bite is prepared. In orthognathic surgery generally, newer tools include surgery-first sequencing, clear aligners as alternatives to long periods of pre-surgical braces, and 3D software that predicts the post-surgical face and helps patients visualise the plan [22][5].

Orthognathic surgery has a long history; Wikipedia cites an early published case by Simon Hullihen in 1849 and describes jaw osteotomies of the 1940s, with Hugo Obwegeser popularising the bilateral sagittal split osteotomy [22]. Obwegeser (1920-2017), an Austrian surgeon trained under Richard Trauner at Graz and influenced by Paul Tessier's midface advancement work, developed a modern Le Fort I osteotomy that fully mobilises the maxilla and described performing maxillary and mandibular surgery together; Wikipedia gives 1969 in the body of his biography and 1970 in the lead for the bimaxillary publication, and notes that he presented his techniques to North American surgeons in 1966 [23].

The use of jaw advancement for breathing began in the late 1970s, when lower-jaw advancement was noticed to reduce sleepiness in three patients [1]. An AI-generated encyclopedia summary credits Riley and Powell at Stanford with a 1986 study showing larger posterior airway gains from two-jaw advancement than from mandibular advancement alone [15]. Published case series from the late 1980s and 1990s reported MMA outcomes in sleep apnoea, including 23 patients treated with Le Fort I and sagittal split osteotomies with rigid fixation, and 50 consecutive patients treated within a site-specific approach [10][11]. A 1994 paper in the journal Sleep reported surgical treatment of sleep apnoea by maxillomandibular advancement [29].

In the Stanford protocol, MMA is described as the second phase of sleep surgery, after phase I procedures on the nose, palate or tongue [2]. Since the 2010s, systematic reviews have pooled outcomes, and research has widened to quality of life, aesthetics and planning methods [3][4][24][25].

A 2010 systematic review and meta-analysis estimated clinical efficacy and safety of MMA from 53 reports describing 22 patient populations and 627 adults.[7] A broader 2010 meta-analysis assessed several upper airway surgeries including MMA for adult sleep apnoea.[6] A 2016 meta-analysis using individual patient data identified criteria associated with surgical outcomes.[4]

The 2025 meta-analysis found significant improvements in apnoea-hypopnoea index, respiratory disturbance index, lowest oxygen saturation and Epworth sleepiness scale, with a small reduction in body mass index.[3] A randomised trial compared MMA with autotitrating positive airway pressure in adults with severe sleep apnoea.[8] A narrative review describes MMA as a possibly unique treatment option with a high probability of cure while describing mandibular advancement devices as a solid option for milder disease.[9]

A 2016 individual-patient-data meta-analysis described MMA as an invasive yet effective surgical option that enlarges the upper airway by physically expanding the facial skeletal framework [4]. The 2025 meta-analysis of 31 studies and 1,597 patients reported changes of about -41.9 events per hour in apnoea-hypopnoea index, -46.2 per hour in respiratory disturbance index, about 6.3 percentage points in lowest oxygen saturation, -8.7 points on the Epworth sleepiness scale and -0.74 kg/m2 in BMI [3]. A trial in the Forli ENT department compared MMA with autotitrating positive airway pressure, which is considered the standard treatment for severe disease [8]. A review states that, with adequate planning and communication, MMA is effective in OSA by objective and subjective measures [2].

A 2025 systematic review in the Angle Orthodontist, drawing on 1,407 retrieved articles of which six entered the quantitative analysis, found that MMA improved patients' subjective quality of life by about 6.4 points on questionnaire scales with long-term stability [25]. A retrospective cohort of 26 patients reported a fall in apnoea-hypopnoea index from about 46 to 6.6 events per hour when advancement was guided by a facial soft-tissue reference called the Barcelona Line; its authors note that the results reflect both advancement magnitude and patient selection and disclose that the lead author proposed the line [28].

Because MMA moves the whole mid and lower face, appearance change is a recognised consequence and sometimes a stated goal. Orthognathic surgery in general is used to correct facial imbalance, asymmetry and malproportion and is described as improving appearance and self-esteem; because the change is usually noticeable, a psychological assessment is sometimes done [22].

A 2023 meta-analysis in Cureus examined satisfaction with facial aesthetics after MMA for sleep apnoea, defining satisfaction as increased fondness for one's appearance or indifference to the change. It searched four databases up to June 2021 and reported a pooled satisfaction of 94.2 percent, with higher aesthetic satisfaction across patient, physician and layperson evaluators [24]. A review of bimaxillary osteotomy for sleep apnoea likewise reports that many patients describe a positive change in facial aesthetics [2].

Not every jaw pattern behaves alike. A 2026 scoping review of nine studies on skeletal Class III patients described three variants, from bimaxillary advancement to maxillary advancement with mandibular setback, and noted that bimaxillary advancement gave the greatest airway enlargement but also the highest risk of facial aesthetic distortion; every variant lowered the apnoea-hypopnoea index by at least half and the authors called for individualised planning [26]. Some surgeons plan advancement against soft-tissue landmarks to balance airway and facial form, as in the Barcelona Line approach [28].

Reviews state that recovery after MMA is longer than after other sleep surgeries because the facial bones must heal in their new position [1]. For orthognathic surgery generally, Wikipedia reports initial healing of 2 to 6 weeks with bone union and remodelling taking a further 2 to 4 months, swelling that can last months, a temporary liquid diet and weight loss, and return to work at 2 to 6 weeks [22]. Antibiotics given around surgery reduce infection risk, which is reported at up to 7 percent [22].
Airway monitoring after surgery, including fibreoptic examination, is discussed in the sleep-surgery literature because postoperative swelling can narrow the airway [5].

Human studies are mainly in sleep apnoea. They include the meta-analyses above, a randomised trial of MMA versus autotitrating positive airway pressure,[8] a clinical trial of how counter-clockwise rotation of the occlusal plane affects mandibular advancement, pharynx shape and polysomnography,[12] and registered studies of quality of life, airway volume and velopharyngeal function after MMA.[13]

Studies of appearance after MMA in non-sleep-apnoea patients were not identified; a review of bimaxillary osteotomy for sleep apnoea reports that many patients describe a positive change in facial aesthetics.[2]

Registered studies include quality of life in 80 OSA patients treated with MMA [17], an 80-patient study of MMA in OSA [18], a long-term outcome study in 12 patients [20], velopharyngeal insufficiency after MMA [19] and a trial of splintless versus conventional MMA [21]. Earlier case series reported 23 patients [10] and 50 consecutive patients [11].

In the 2025 meta-analysis the most frequent sequelae were early lower-facial numbness (about 83 percent), later numbness (about 67 percent before one year and 33 percent beyond one year) and hardware removal (about 22 percent); higher preoperative body mass index correlated with longer hospital stay.[3] Reviews also describe airway monitoring after surgery and complications specific to MMA that are weighed against its benefit.[5][2]

The 2025 meta-analysis also found a positive correlation between preoperative body mass index and length of hospital stay [3]. Procedure-specific complications and airway monitoring after surgery are discussed in the reviews [2][5].

Orthognathic surgery in general carries risks of bleeding, swelling, infection and nerve injury causing facial numbness that is usually temporary but rarely permanent; some movements, such as maxillary impaction, carry higher risk [22]. Reviews of skeletal sleep surgery weigh these risks against the benefit in patients who cannot use positive airway pressure [16][27].

On looksmax.org, MMA appears in threads that ask how the operation affects other facial changes, for example whether it would undo cheek width gained from maxillary skeletal expansion; users in the thread name surgeons and share opinions without published data to support them.[14]

Terms common in these communities include bimax or Bi-Max for double-jaw surgery, MSE for miniscrew-assisted maxillary skeletal expansion and SFOT for subsequent surgically assisted expansion; users mention surgeons by name and trade experiences, but these discussions are anecdotal [14].

Discussions often frame jaw surgery in terms of forward growth, midface support and jawline definition. Published orthognathic and sleep-surgery literature describes the same skeletal movement in terms of airway enlargement, bite correction and aesthetic satisfaction [22][24][27].

MMA is related to isolated bimaxillary orthognathic surgery for dentofacial deformity, to genioplasty and genioglossus advancement, to maxillary expansion and to hypoglossal nerve stimulation and mandibular advancement devices as sleep-apnoea alternatives [1][9][22]. Other skeletal options, including mandibular distraction, are covered in sleep-surgery reviews [16].

timeline.event: Simon Hullihen publishes an early case of jaw surgery, according to Wikipedia's orthognathic article.[22]
Hugo Obwegeser presents his orthognathic techniques to North American surgeons in Washington, D.C.[23]
Obwegeser describes combined maxillary and mandibular surgery (Le Fort I with sagittal split); sources differ on the year.[23]
Lower-jaw advancement is observed to reduce sleepiness in three patients, according to Wikipedia.[1]
Riley and Powell at Stanford report greater airway gains from two-jaw advancement, according to an AI-generated encyclopedia overview.[15]
A series of 23 patients with sleep apnoea treated by MMA with rigid fixation is published.[10]
A paper on surgical treatment of sleep apnoea by maxillomandibular advancement appears in Sleep.[29]
A series of 50 consecutive patients treated with MMA is published.[11]
Systematic reviews and meta-analyses pool MMA outcomes for sleep apnoea.[6][7]
A meta-analysis reports a pooled 94.2 percent satisfaction with facial aesthetics after MMA.[24]
A meta-analysis of 31 studies reports AHI improvement and common sequelae.[3]
Reviews and a scoping review address contemporary practice and skeletal Class III patients.[26][27]

lore.intro: MMA is discussed on forums mostly as part of broader jaw-surgery planning, with questions about interaction with maxillary expansion and surgeon choice.[14]

claims.claim: MMA after skeletal expansion could cause the cheeks to drop and lose expansion gains.
claims.believers: A forum poster who had miniscrew-assisted expansion asks whether later MMA will cost them cheek gains.[14]
claims.experts: No published studies were identified that examine MMA after maxillary skeletal expansion for cheek appearance; the sleep literature discusses maxillary expansion as a separate emerging option within MMA planning.[2]

claims.claim: Moving both jaws forward gives a looks improvement together with an airway benefit.
claims.believers: Forum discussions describe jaw advancement as serving appearance and breathing at once.[14]
claims.experts: Meta-analyses document large reductions in apnoea-hypopnoea index after MMA in OSA patients, and a review reports that many patients also describe an aesthetic improvement.[2][3]

claims.claim: Bimax produces forward growth and a more defined face while also fixing breathing.
claims.believers: Forum posters discuss jaw advancement as serving appearance and airway together, often alongside expansion and chin work.[14]
claims.experts: Reviews report large airway gains in sleep-apnoea patients, and a meta-analysis pooled 94.2 percent satisfaction with facial aesthetics; the scoping review of Class III patients notes aesthetic distortion risk with bimaxillary advancement in some jaw patterns.[24][26]

claims.claim: MMA numbness and hardware problems are minor and short-lived.
claims.believers: Some patients and forum users describe recovery as manageable and the result as worth it.[14]
claims.experts: The 2025 meta-analysis found early lower-facial numbness in about 83 percent of patients, persisting beyond a year in about a third, and hardware removal in about 22 percent.[3]

claims.claim: Surgeon choice determines the aesthetic result.
claims.believers: Thread participants name individual surgeons and treat selection as decisive for the final look.[14]
claims.experts: Reviews emphasise careful planning, including soft-tissue-guided planning and virtual surgical planning, and one soft-tissue-guided study notes its results reflect both technique and patient selection.[5][28]

angle.text: MMA changes the position of the whole lower face by moving both jaws. Surgeons use it chiefly for sleep apnoea and bite problems, and a review reports that many patients describe a positive change in facial aesthetics.
